files..cargo/config.toml:
# A Windows tiny.exe runs on a machine with nothing else installed: the C
# runtime is linked into it, rather than expected to be there already as the
# Visual C++ Redistributable. A fresh Windows does not have that, and the
# binary would stop at "VCRUNTIME140.dll was not found" before drawing a thing.
#
# The C that tiny compiles — the map's parsers, and Lua — follows the same
# setting, so everything in the binary agrees on which runtime it has.
[target.x86_64-pc-windows-msvc]
rustflags = ["-C", "target-feature=+crt-static"]

[target.aarch64-pc-windows-msvc]
rustflags = ["-C", "target-feature=+crt-static"]
files..github/workflows/ci.yml:
# The three platforms tiny claims to run on, on every push.
#
# The claim is the point. tiny is developed on Linux, so "it works on Windows
# and macOS" is otherwise a thing nobody has watched happen — and the ways it
# breaks are exactly the ones a Linux machine cannot show you: a `\` where a `/`
# was expected, a temp directory that is a symlink, a short name like
# `RUNNER~1`, a shell that turns stderr into an error.
name: ci

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

# Nothing here writes anything back; only the release workflow needs to.
permissions:
  contents: read

# A second push while the first is still building makes the first answer moot.
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

env:
  CARGO_TERM_COLOR: always

jobs:
  test:
    name: test on ${{ matrix.os }}
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      # Every platform runs even when one fails: which ones broke is the
      # information worth having.
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Install the toolchain
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          components: rustfmt, clippy

      - uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2

      # The git window shells out to git, and its tests build real
      # repositories. A committer has to exist for `git commit` to work, and
      # the runners do not set one globally.
      - name: Give git a name
        run: |
          git config --global user.email ci@example.com
          git config --global user.name CI

      # `--locked` everywhere: without it cargo quietly re-resolves, so a
      # Cargo.lock that has fallen behind Cargo.toml passes every check here
      # and then fails the tagged release build, which is the one build that
      # cannot simply be run again.
      - run: cargo fmt --all -- --check
      - run: cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings
      - run: cargo test --locked --all-targets
      - run: cargo build --locked --release

      # The docs are half this codebase and they can break: an intra-doc link
      # to something that has been renamed is a warning, and warnings are easy
      # to walk past locally. Not on the matrix by accident — some items are
      # behind `cfg(windows)`, and their links only resolve where they compile.
      - name: Check the documentation
        env:
          RUSTDOCFLAGS: -D warnings
        run: cargo doc --locked --no-deps --document-private-items

  # `rust-version` in Cargo.toml is a promise, and `install.sh` will build with
  # whatever `cargo` it finds — including the older one a distribution ships.
  # This is the job that keeps the promise true.
  msrv:
    name: build on the oldest Rust we claim
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # Read from the manifest rather than written down again here, so the
      # version cannot be raised in one place and not the other.
      - name: Read rust-version from Cargo.toml
        id: msrv
        run: |
          version=$(grep -m1 '^rust-version' Cargo.toml | tr -d '"[:space:]' | cut -d= -f2)
          echo "claimed: $version"
          echo "version=$version" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          toolchain: ${{ steps.msrv.outputs.version }}

      - uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2

      - run: cargo check --locked --all-targets

  installers:
    name: parse the installers on ${{ matrix.os }}
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Parse install.sh
        if: runner.os != 'Windows'
        # `sh -n` on the platform's own shell: dash on Linux, bash-as-sh on
        # macOS. A GNU-only spelling fails here rather than on someone's Mac.
        run: sh -n install.sh

      # Both PowerShells. 5.1 is the one every copy of Windows has, and it
      # reads a script file differently from 7 — which is how a script that
      # parsed perfectly in 7 could still fail on a real machine.
      - name: Parse install.ps1 in PowerShell 7
        if: runner.os == 'Windows'
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          $errors = $null
          [System.Management.Automation.Language.Parser]::ParseFile(
            "$PWD\install.ps1", [ref]$null, [ref]$errors) | Out-Null
          if ($errors) { $errors | ForEach-Object { Write-Host $_ }; exit 1 }
          Write-Host 'install.ps1 parses in PowerShell 7'

      - name: Parse install.ps1 in Windows PowerShell 5.1
        if: runner.os == 'Windows'
        shell: powershell
        run: |
          $errors = $null
          [System.Management.Automation.Language.Parser]::ParseFile(
            "$PWD\install.ps1", [ref]$null, [ref]$errors) | Out-Null
          if ($errors) { $errors | ForEach-Object { Write-Host $_ }; exit 1 }
          Write-Host 'install.ps1 parses in Windows PowerShell 5.1'

      - name: Keep install.ps1 plain ASCII
        if: runner.os != 'Windows'
        # 5.1 reads a local .ps1 in the ANSI code page, where one byte of a
        # UTF-8 em dash is a curly quote that ends a string early.
        run: |
          if LC_ALL=C grep -n '[^ -~]' install.ps1; then
            echo "install.ps1 must be plain ASCII (lines above)"; exit 1
          fi

  # The installers end to end, the way someone would run them — from a
  # directory that is not the checkout, so they take the real path: download
  # the release if there is one, otherwise clone the branch and build it.
  # Pushes only, because a pull request's merge ref is not a branch the
  # installer can clone by name.
  install-windows:
    name: install on Windows (PowerShell 5.1)
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: windows-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Run install.ps1
        shell: powershell
        env:
          TINY_REF: ${{ github.ref_name }}
          TINY_PREFIX: ${{ runner.temp }}\tinybin
          # Build, do not download. Once a release exists the installer would
          # rightly prefer it, and this job would quietly stop testing the
          # commit that was just pushed — which is the whole point of it.
          TINY_FROM_SOURCE: 1
        run: |
          Set-Location $env:RUNNER_TEMP
          & "$env:GITHUB_WORKSPACE\install.ps1"
          if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { exit 1 }
          & "$env:TINY_PREFIX\tiny.exe" --version
          if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { exit 1 }

  install-macos:
    name: install on macOS
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: macos-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Run install.sh
        env:
          TINY_REF: ${{ github.ref_name }}
          TINY_PREFIX: ${{ runner.temp }}/tinybin
          # Build rather than download, for the reason above.
          TINY_FROM_SOURCE: 1
        run: |
          cd "$RUNNER_TEMP"
          sh "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE/install.sh"
          "$TINY_PREFIX/tiny" --version

  install-linux:
    name: install on Linux
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Run install.sh
        env:
          TINY_REF: ${{ github.ref_name }}
          TINY_PREFIX: ${{ runner.temp }}/tinybin
          # Build rather than download, for the reason above.
          TINY_FROM_SOURCE: 1
        run: |
          cd "$RUNNER_TEMP"
          sh "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE/install.sh"
          "$TINY_PREFIX/tiny" --version

  # The install line exactly as the README gives it: nothing forced, so it
  # takes the newest release for the machine it is on, and builds only where
  # there is none. The three jobs above test the commit; this one tests the
  # line on the front page, on all three systems it promises.
  install-release:
    name: one-line install on ${{ matrix.os }}
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Run install.sh
        if: runner.os != 'Windows'
        env:
          TINY_PREFIX: ${{ runner.temp }}/tinybin
        run: |
          cd "$RUNNER_TEMP"
          sh "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE/install.sh"
          "$TINY_PREFIX/tiny" --version
      - name: Run install.ps1
        if: runner.os == 'Windows'
        shell: powershell
        env:
          TINY_PREFIX: ${{ runner.temp }}\tinybin
        run: |
          Set-Location $env:RUNNER_TEMP
          & "$env:GITHUB_WORKSPACE\install.ps1"
          if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { exit 1 }
          & "$env:TINY_PREFIX\tiny.exe" --version
          if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { exit 1 }

  # The README leads with screenshots, and a moved file turns them into broken
  # images on the front page of the project — which is the one page everybody
  # sees and nobody tests.
  pictures:
    name: the README's pictures are there
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Every image the README points at
        run: |
          missing=0
          for image in $(grep -o 'docs/[A-Za-z0-9_-]*\.png' README.md | sort -u); do
            if [ -f "$image" ]; then
              echo "ok      $image"
            else
              echo "MISSING $image"
              missing=1
            fi
          done
          exit $missing
files..github/workflows/release.yml:
# Ready-made binaries: built on every push to main, published when a version
# is tagged.
#
# This is what makes tiny installable on a machine with no compiler. Building
# from source needs Rust, and on Windows it also needs the Visual Studio Build
# Tools — several gigabytes, an administrator prompt and twenty minutes, to try
# a seven-megabyte program. A Mac needs the Xcode command line tools for the
# same reason. The installers download one of these instead, and only fall back
# to building when there is none for the machine.
#
# Every push to main runs all of it except the publishing, so by the time a
# version is tagged its exact build has already passed here. To release:
#
#   1. Set `version` in Cargo.toml, and give it a section in CHANGELOG.md.
#   2. Push to main, and wait for this and `ci` to pass.
#   3. git tag v0.4.5 && git push origin v0.4.5
#
# The tag has to match Cargo.toml and the changelog has to have the version in
# it — the `version` job stops the release before anything is built otherwise.
name: release

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    tags: ['v*']
  # Runs the builds by hand, to check the packaging without publishing. Only a
  # tag publishes; see the `publish` job's condition.
  workflow_dispatch:

# Building needs nothing more. The one job that writes asks for it itself.
permissions:
  contents: read

# A dry run on main is made moot by the next push. A release is never cut
# short half way through.
concurrency:
  group: release-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref_type == 'branch' }}

env:
  CARGO_TERM_COLOR: always

jobs:
  version:
    name: check the version
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      version: ${{ steps.read.outputs.version }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Read the version, and hold the tag and the changelog to it
        id: read
        run: |
          version=$(grep -m1 '^version' Cargo.toml | cut -d'"' -f2)
          echo "Cargo.toml says $version"
          echo "version=$version" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          if [ "$GITHUB_REF_TYPE" = tag ] && [ "$GITHUB_REF_NAME" != "v$version" ]; then
            echo "::error::the tag is $GITHUB_REF_NAME but Cargo.toml says $version"
            exit 1
          fi
          if ! grep -q "^## $version " CHANGELOG.md; then
            echo "::error::CHANGELOG.md has no section for $version"
            exit 1
          fi

  build:
    name: build ${{ matrix.target }}
    needs: version
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          - os: windows-latest
            target: x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
          # Apple silicon natively, and Intel cross-built on the same runner:
          # Apple's toolchain builds both, and Intel runners are going away.
          - os: macos-latest
            target: aarch64-apple-darwin
          - os: macos-latest
            target: x86_64-apple-darwin
            cross: true
          # The oldest Ubuntu GitHub still runs, because a binary runs on the
          # C library it was linked against *or newer*. install.sh tries the
          # download before keeping it, and builds instead where it will not
          # start.
          - os: ubuntu-22.04
            target: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
          - os: ubuntu-22.04-arm
            target: aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          targets: ${{ matrix.target }}

      - uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with:
          key: ${{ matrix.target }}

      - run: cargo build --release --locked --target ${{ matrix.target }}

      # A binary that does not start, or calls itself a different version,
      # is caught here rather than on someone's machine.
      - name: Run it
        if: ${{ !matrix.cross }}
        shell: bash
        run: |
          got=$("target/${{ matrix.target }}/release/tiny" --version)
          echo "$got"
          [ "$got" = "tiny ${{ needs.version.outputs.version }}" ]

      - name: Check it is built for Intel
        if: ${{ matrix.cross }}
        run: lipo -info "target/${{ matrix.target }}/release/tiny" | grep x86_64

      # The names here are what the installers ask for — `tiny-<target>.zip` on
      # Windows, `tiny-<target>.tar.gz` everywhere else — so change them in both
      # places or neither. The notices go beside the license: the binary
      # carries other people's work, and theirs travel with it.
      - name: Package for Windows
        if: runner.os == 'Windows'
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          $bin = "target/${{ matrix.target }}/release/tiny.exe"
          Compress-Archive -Path $bin, README.md, LICENSE, THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt `
            -DestinationPath "tiny-${{ matrix.target }}.zip"

      - name: Package for macOS and Linux
        if: runner.os != 'Windows'
        run: |
          tar -czf "tiny-${{ matrix.target }}.tar.gz" \
            -C "target/${{ matrix.target }}/release" tiny \
            -C "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE" README.md LICENSE THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: tiny-${{ matrix.target }}
          path: tiny-${{ matrix.target }}.*

  publish:
    name: publish the release
    needs: [version, build]
    # A push to main or a hand-run build has no tag to hang a release on; it
    # stops here with the packages downloadable from the run page.
    if: github.ref_type == 'tag'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          path: dist
          merge-multiple: true

      - name: Checksums
        working-directory: dist
        run: sha256sum * | tee SHA256SUMS

      # The release notes are the version's own section of the changelog, so
      # the two can never say different things.
      - name: Release notes
        run: |
          awk -v v="${{ needs.version.outputs.version }}" '
            index($0, "## " v " ") == 1 { inside = 1; next }
            inside && /^## / { exit }
            inside { print }
          ' CHANGELOG.md > notes.md
          cat notes.md
          [ -s notes.md ]

      - uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v3
        with:
          name: tiny ${{ needs.version.outputs.version }}
          body_path: notes.md
          files: dist/*
files.CHANGELOG.md:
# Changelog

Each version is a `v` tag, with ready-made binaries on its
[release page](https://github.com/mattsaund/tiny/releases).

## 0.5.1 - 2026-10-21

- **Every heading level renders.** `###` and deeper used to show their
  hashes. They fade by depth now, bold to dim, with no markup showing through
  and no extra rules on the page.
- **Tabs are drawn.** A tab reached the screen as a cell holding nothing, so
  a tab indented file lost its shape and a tab between two words joined them.
  Tabs now expand to their stops everywhere: the editor, the preview, markdown
  and the git diff. Makefiles and Go keep their indentation.

## 0.5.0 — 2026-10-11

- **Commands are sentences.** `*copy temp.txt to notes`, `*goto function
  main`, `*goto word todo in notes.md`, `*replace hi with hello`. Many ways to
  say each (`go to`, `open`, `jump to`; `remove`, `rm`; `change … to`), and
  every older spelling still works.
- **The bar says what Enter will do** on the line under it, with counts —
  before anything happens.
- **Names from anywhere.** `notes` is the folder called notes wherever it is;
  `readme` finds README.md. Two with one name are listed, not guessed.
- **goto** a line, function, word, text, heading, file or folder — in one file
  with `in a.md`, otherwise across the project. Again goes to the next one.
- **replace** is whole words. With no `in` it does the whole project and asks
  first; `in a.md` changes that file, and `Ctrl+Z` undoes it.
- `*open map`, `*show git`, `*help` open those windows.
- Updating no longer prints the first-install advice.
- **Third-party notices.** `tiny --licenses`, and every download, carry the
  copyright and license of everything compiled in: each crate, Lua, and the
  color themes.

## 0.4.6 — 2026-10-11

- **A much faster project map.** Opening it reads files on every core and
  skips the ones with nothing to find in them, like pictures. A 20,000-note
  vault opens in half a second instead of three, and a 25,000-file code
  folder in about five instead of thirty. Moving around it takes
  milliseconds, not two seconds a key.
- **Faster search.** Files are read on every core, a lowercase search is no
  slower than one with capitals, and fast typing searches once rather than
  once a letter. Up to 10× quicker on big folders.
- **Faster notes.** Code blocks in markdown draw quicker.
- **Fixes:** maps of very large projects lay out correctly; `tiny
  --licenses` lists the crates only the Windows build uses.

## 0.4.5 — 2026-10-10

- **Releases.** Ready-made tiny for macOS, Linux and Windows, Intel and ARM.
  The install line downloads it; no Rust needed. The installers also offer
  git and ffmpeg (and xdg-utils on Linux) if they are missing, and Windows
  needs no Visual C++ runtime.
- **Updates.** tiny says when a new version is out, and `y` installs it.
  Also `tiny --update` and `*update`. `update_check = false` stops it asking.
- **Plugins.** Lua files in the plugins folder add commands and react to
  opening and saving. Settings → `Plugins` opens the folder; `*reload` loads
  new ones.
- **Keys that work on every terminal**, macOS Terminal included: `?` help,
  `Ctrl+G` git, `Ctrl+L` map, `Ctrl+T` browser, `Ctrl+F` search, `Ctrl+A` /
  `Ctrl+E` line ends, `Ctrl+U` / `Ctrl+D` page, `⌥←` / `⌥→` words, `<` / `>`
  browser width. No function keys, Ctrl+digits or Ctrl+arrows needed.
- **`Ctrl+N`** opens another tiny on the same project, in a new window.
- **Windows:** file paste is `Ctrl+P`, since Windows Terminal keeps `Ctrl+V`.
- **PDFs and audio** open in your own viewer on Enter, like pictures and video.
- **Keybinds, settings and help:** fewer words, no duplicate keys. Key names
  from older configs still work.

## 0.3.1 and earlier

Before releases — see the git history.

version = "0.5.1"
edition = "2024"
# Let-chains, which this uses throughout, landed in 1.88.
rust-version = "1.88"
description = "A personal knowledge manager that lives entirely in the terminal"
repository = "https://github.com/mattsaund/tiny"
license = "MIT"
readme = "README.md"
keywords = ["tui", "notes", "markdown", "knowledge-management", "editor"]
categories = ["command-line-utilities", "text-editors"]

[dependencies]
anyhow = "1.0.104"
crossterm = "0.29.0"
# Plugins. Lua 5.4 is compiled into the binary from source (`vendored`), so a
# plugin needs nothing installed to run — see `plugins`.
mlua = { version = "0.12.1", default-features = false, features = ["lua54", "vendored"] }
pulldown-cmark = { version = "0.13.4", default-features = false }
ratatui = "0.30.2"
serde = { version = "1.0.229", features = ["derive"] }
syntect = { version = "5.3.0", default-features = false, features = ["parsing", "default-themes", "dump-load", "regex-fancy"] }
toml = "1.1.4"
tree-sitter-javascript = "0.25.0"
tree-sitter-python = "0.25.0"
tree-sitter-rust = "0.24.2"
tree-sitter-tags = "0.26.13"
two-face = { version = "0.5.2", default-features = false, features = ["syntect-fancy"] }
unicode-width = "0.2.2"

[dev-dependencies]
# Reads `cargo metadata` when the third-party notices are written — see
# `licenses`. Already in the build for other crates; never in the binary.
serde_json = "1.0.151"
tempfile = "3.27.0"

# Release is what people install, and they wait for it: `install.sh` builds
# from source on their machine, so this profile is the install time.
#
# Thin LTO still lets the optimizer see across crate boundaries — which matters
# here because the hot loop (syntect's regex matching, called from `highlight`)
# sits behind two of them — but it does the work per-module and in parallel
# instead of merging the whole program into one unit. With sixteen codegen
# units to go at, that is the difference between a 42-second install and a
# 19-second one, measured on a clean build of the full dependency graph. It
# costs about 0.7 MB of binary, which is the trade this project has chosen:
# nobody notices the megabyte, everybody notices the wait.
#
# `strip` drops symbols that only a debugger would want, and takes about 2 MB
# off the binary.
[profile.release]
lto = "thin"
codegen-units = 16
strip = true
# No unwinding. A panic in tiny is a bug with nothing to recover to — nothing
# catches one, and the terminal is given back by a hook rather than by a
# destructor (see `hand_back_the_terminal_on_panic`), so unwinding was only
# ever paying for tables nobody read. Dropping them is 0.42 MB of the binary.
# Tests are built with the dev profile and still unwind, so `#[should_panic]`
# would go on working if anything here ever wanted it.
panic = "abort"

# tiny

Tiny is an IDE, text editor, personal knowledge management system, and file
browser that lives in the terminal. Search, git, a project map and plugins are
built in. Plain files in plain folders; nothing proprietary.

**Full installation size:** 7.54 MB macOS (Intel), 7.15 MB macOS (Apple
silicon), 8.32 MB Linux (x86_64), 7.78 MB Linux (arm64), 7.78 MB Windows

Try it here: https://msaunders.dev/tiny/

![tiny editing its own source](docs/browser.png)

## Install

**Linux, macOS**

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mattsaund/tiny/main/install.sh | sh
```

**Windows**

```powershell
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mattsaund/tiny/main/install.ps1 | iex
```

Downloads the newest [release](https://github.com/mattsaund/tiny/releases) for
your machine (or builds it), and offers git and ffmpeg if they are missing.
tiny tells you when a new version is out, and `y` updates it. `tiny --update` does
the same; `tiny --uninstall` removes tiny and leaves your files alone.
What changed: [CHANGELOG](CHANGELOG.md).

## Use

```sh
tiny                 # this folder
tiny ~/notes         # that folder, made if it is missing
tiny ~/code/main.py  # that file
```

## Search everything

![searching the project](docs/search.png)

`/` searches names and contents as you type. Start with `*` for a command.

## Git

![the git window](docs/git.png)

`Ctrl+G`. `Enter` stages, `commit` commits, with the git you already have.

## Project map

![the project map](docs/map.png)

`Ctrl+L`. Wikilinks, markdown links and calls between files: green reaches
this file, red is what it reaches.

## Notes, pictures, PDFs

![markdown, rendered](docs/markdown.png)

Markdown renders as you read it; `Enter` edits. Headings at every level,
tables, fenced code with syntax colors, quotes and task lists. Pictures, video,
audio and PDFs open in your own viewer.

## Keys

`?` shows every key.

| key | does |
|---|---|
| arrows, `i` `j` `k` `l` | move |
| `Enter`, `Esc` | open, back |
| `Ctrl+S` | save (on a folder, all of it) |
| `/`, `Ctrl+F` | search |
| `Ctrl+G`, `Ctrl+L` | git, map |
| `Ctrl+T`, `<` `>` | hide the browser, its width |
| `Ctrl+N` | another tiny window |
| `Ctrl+Q` | quit |

## Commands

Say it in words. The line under the bar says what Enter will do.

```
*goto line 42                 *copy temp.txt to notes
*goto function main           *move temp.txt to notes
*goto word todo in a.md       *rename old.md to new.md
*goto file notes.md           *new notes/today.md
*replace hi with hello        *delete old.md
*replace hi with hey in a.md  *set tab_width to 2
```

Names are found anywhere in the project. No `in` means everywhere. `go to`,
`open`, `cp`, `rm`, `*42` and the rest work too.

## Plugins

A plugin is a Lua file in the plugins folder, which `Plugins` in settings
opens. Drop one in and `*reload`.

```lua
-- words.lua: *words counts them
tiny.command("words", function()
  local n = 0
  for _ in tiny.text():gmatch("%S+") do n = n + 1 end
  tiny.status(n .. " words")
end)
```

`tiny.command` `tiny.on("open"/"save")` `tiny.status` `tiny.text`
`tiny.set_text` `tiny.insert` `tiny.cursor` `tiny.go` `tiny.path` `tiny.root`
`tiny.open`

## Config

`*config` opens the settings; `tiny --config` prints where `tiny.conf` is.
Keys go in `[keys]`:

```toml
[keys]
down        = "z"
editor.undo = "ctrl+u"
```

## Contributing

**AI policy.** I am open to AI and agentic coding, but the code written needs
to follow specific guidelines:

1. MUST be human readable, acceptable variable/function names.
2. Easily traceable, following a good program flow.
3. Contributors MUST look at and document code and code changes. You need to
   understand the code that is being written.

**Tests.** `cargo test`, `cargo clippy` and `cargo fmt`. CI runs all three on
Linux, macOS and Windows. A version is released by tagging it; see
`.github/workflows/release.yml`.

#!/bin/sh
# Install tiny — a terminal knowledge manager.
#
#   curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mattsaund/tiny/main/install.sh | sh
#
# It downloads the ready-made binary from the latest GitHub release, for macOS
# or Linux, Intel or ARM. Only when there is none for this machine, or it will
# not run here, or this is run from inside a checkout, does it build from
# source — fetching the source itself when piped from the web.
#
# Then it offers what tiny reaches for while it runs — git for the git window,
# ffmpeg for video and audio details, xdg-utils to open files on Linux — with
# the system's own package manager, in one question. tiny runs without them.
#
# Override anything with the environment:
#   TINY_REPO=...         git URL to clone
#   TINY_REF=...          branch or tag (default: main); a version tag like
#                         v0.4.5 installs that release
#   TINY_PREFIX=...       where the binary lands (default: ~/.local/bin)
#   TINY_FROM_SOURCE=1    build even where a download is available

set -eu

REPO="${TINY_REPO:-https://github.com/mattsaund/tiny.git}"
REF="${TINY_REF:-main}"
PREFIX="${TINY_PREFIX:-$HOME/.local/bin}"

say() { printf '%s\n' "$*"; }
die() { printf 'install: %s\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }
have() { command -v "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1; }

# A yes-or-no question, where Enter means yes. It reads from the terminal
# rather than stdin, because piped from the web stdin is this script, and a
# `read` from there would take its next line as the answer. With no terminal to
# ask, the answer is no.
ask() {
    printf '  [Y/n] '
    if [ -t 0 ]; then reply_src=/dev/stdin; else reply_src=/dev/tty; fi
    { read -r reply < "$reply_src"; } 2>/dev/null || { reply=n; printf '\n'; }
    case "${reply:-y}" in [Nn]*) return 1 ;; esac
}

# A temporary directory, and a temporary file.
#
# `mktemp -d` with no template is a GNU extension. BSD's — which is macOS's —
# wants either a template or `-t`, and exits with a usage message otherwise, so
# a script that only knows the GNU spelling dies on a Mac before it has done
# anything. Try the short form, fall back to the form both understand.
temp_dir() { mktemp -d 2>/dev/null || mktemp -d -t tiny; }
temp_file() { mktemp 2>/dev/null || mktemp -t tiny; }

# Everything to clean up on the way out, however we leave. One trap, because a
# second `trap ... EXIT` would silently replace the first.
SRC=""
SRC_IS_TEMP=""
LOG=""
ROOT=""
cleanup() {
    [ -n "$SRC_IS_TEMP" ] && [ -n "$SRC" ] && rm -rf "$SRC"
    [ -n "$LOG" ] && rm -f "$LOG"
    [ -n "$ROOT" ] && rm -rf "$ROOT"
    return 0
}
trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM

# Whether it is worth drawing anything that moves. A log file, a CI job or a
# pipe gets plain lines instead — a progress bar redrawn with carriage returns
# into a file is a single unreadable line thousands of characters long.
tty_out() { [ -t 1 ] && [ "${TERM:-dumb}" != dumb ]; }

# Put the binary at $1 in $PREFIX, over whatever tiny is already there.
#
# Copied in beside the old one and renamed over it. A rename replaces a program
# even while it runs — which it is, when tiny is updating itself — without
# touching the copy it is running from; writing over it in place would not,
# and a copy from a temporary directory on another disk is a write.
put_in_place() {
    mkdir -p "$PREFIX" \
        && cp "$1" "$PREFIX/.tiny.new" \
        && chmod +x "$PREFIX/.tiny.new" \
        && mv -f "$PREFIX/.tiny.new" "$PREFIX/tiny" \
        || { rm -f "$PREFIX/.tiny.new"; return 1; }
}

# --- the system's package manager ---------------------------------------------

# The package manager this system has, by the name of its command — the
# distribution's own first, Homebrew last. Nothing when there is none.
package_manager() {
    for pm in apt-get dnf pacman zypper apk brew; do
        if have "$pm"; then
            echo "$pm"
            return 0
        fi
    done
}

# Run a command as root: directly when we are, through sudo when we are not.
# sudo asks for its password on the terminal, which works piped from the web.
as_root() {
    if [ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ]; then
        "$@"
    elif have sudo; then
        sudo "$@"
    else
        say "installing needs root, and there is no sudo"
        return 1
    fi
}

# What `$2` is called by the package manager `$1`, where it is not the same
# word everywhere. `cc` stands for "a C compiler", whatever provides one.
package_name() {
    case "$1:$2" in
        dnf:ffmpeg) echo ffmpeg-free ;;
        apt-get:cc) echo build-essential ;;
        pacman:cc) echo base-devel ;;
        apk:cc) echo build-base ;;
        *:cc) echo gcc ;;
        *) echo "$2" ;;
    esac
}

# Install packages, by tiny's names for them, with the package manager `$1`.
install_packages() {
    pm=$1
    shift
    names=""
    for p in "$@"; do names="$names $(package_name "$pm" "$p")"; done
    # `$names` is split into words on purpose: one package per word.
    case "$pm" in
        apt-get) as_root apt-get update -qq && as_root apt-get install -y $names ;;
        dnf) as_root dnf install -y $names ;;
        pacman) as_root pacman -S --needed --noconfirm $names ;;
        zypper) as_root zypper --non-interactive install $names ;;
        apk) as_root apk add $names ;;
        # Homebrew refuses to run as root, and does not need to.
        brew) brew install $names ;;
        *) return 1 ;;
    esac
}

# --- what tiny reaches for while it runs ----------------------------------------
#
# tiny runs on its own. Three programs make parts of it work, and those that
# are missing are offered together, in one question:
#
#   git        the git window
#   ffprobe    the size and length of a video or a song (part of ffmpeg)
#   xdg-open   handing a picture or a PDF to the desktop (Linux)
#
# A no, or no way to install them, leaves tiny working without them. Not asked
# again when tiny is updating itself: that was answered when it was installed.
offer_extras() {
    [ -z "${TINY_UPDATE:-}" ] || return 0
    nl='
'
    missing=""
    why=""
    if [ "$(uname -s)" = Darwin ]; then
        # The git a fresh Mac has is a stand-in that asks for Apple's command
        # line tools, so their presence is the question to ask.
        if ! xcode-select -p >/dev/null 2>&1 && ! [ -x /opt/homebrew/bin/git ] \
            && ! [ -x /usr/local/bin/git ]; then
            say ""
            say "The git window needs git, which comes with Apple's command line"
            say "tools. Install them now?"
            if ask; then
                xcode-select --install >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
                say "finish in the window that opened; tiny works meanwhile"
            fi
        fi
    else
        if ! have git; then
            missing="$missing git"
            why="$why${nl}  git        the git window"
        fi
        if [ -n "${DISPLAY:-}${WAYLAND_DISPLAY:-}" ] && ! have xdg-open; then
            missing="$missing xdg-utils"
            why="$why${nl}  xdg-utils  opening pictures and PDFs"
        fi
    fi
    if ! have ffprobe; then
        missing="$missing ffmpeg"
        why="$why${nl}  ffmpeg     the size and length of videos and songs"
    fi
    [ -n "$missing" ] || return 0

    say ""
    say "tiny can also use these, which are not installed:$why"
    pm=$(package_manager)
    if [ -z "$pm" ]; then
        say "install them to turn those on — tiny works without them"
        return 0
    fi
    say "Install them with $pm?"
    if ! ask; then
        say "skipped — tiny works without them"
        return 0
    fi
    # `$missing` is split into words on purpose: one package per word.
    install_packages "$pm" $missing \
        || say "not all of them installed — tiny works without them"
}

# What to say once there is a binary, from either route to one.
finish() {
    offer_extras
    say ""
    say "installed $PREFIX/tiny"
    # tiny updating itself already knows where it is and how to start; it
    # says so itself, straight after this.
    [ -z "${TINY_UPDATE:-}" ] || return 0
    case ":$PATH:" in
        *":$PREFIX:"*)
            say "run it with:      tiny ~/notes"
            say "remove it with:   tiny --uninstall"
            ;;
        *)
            say "$PREFIX is not on your PATH. Add it:"
            say ""
            case "${SHELL##*/}" in
                fish) say "  fish_add_path $PREFIX" ;;
                zsh)  say "  echo 'export PATH=\"$PREFIX:\$PATH\"' >> ~/.zshrc" ;;
                *)    say "  echo 'export PATH=\"$PREFIX:\$PATH\"' >> ~/.bashrc" ;;
            esac
            say ""
            say "then run:  tiny ~/notes"
            say ""
            say "to remove tiny later:  tiny --uninstall"
            ;;
    esac
}

# --- a ready-made binary -----------------------------------------------------
#
# Building needs Rust, and on a Mac the Xcode command line tools as well — a
# large download to try a small program — so this takes the binary the release
# workflow built, and only builds when there is none to take.
#
# A Linux binary is linked against the C library of the system that built it,
# and will not start on an older one, or on a different one — Alpine's musl.
# So it is asked its version before it replaces anything, and a binary that
# cannot answer is a reason to build instead.
#
# Not when asked to build, and not for a branch: a branch today is not what any
# release was. A version tag names its release exactly, and `main` means the
# newest one.
prebuilt() {
    [ -z "${TINY_FROM_SOURCE:-}" ] || return 1
    case "$REF" in
        main) release=latest/download ;;
        v[0-9]*) release="download/$REF" ;;
        *) return 1 ;;
    esac
    have curl || return 1
    case "$(uname -s)" in
        Darwin) os=apple-darwin ;;
        Linux) os=unknown-linux-gnu ;;
        *) return 1 ;;
    esac
    case "$(uname -m)" in
        arm64|aarch64) arch=aarch64 ;;
        x86_64|amd64) arch=x86_64 ;;
        *) return 1 ;;
    esac
    slug=${REPO#https://github.com/}
    slug=${slug%.git}
    case "$slug" in *://*|*/*/*) return 1 ;; */*) ;; *) return 1 ;; esac
    url="https://github.com/$slug/releases/$release/tiny-$arch-$os.tar.gz"
    dir="$(temp_dir)" || return 1
    printf 'downloading tiny for %s ... ' "$arch-$os"
    if ! curl -fsSL "$url" -o "$dir/tiny.tar.gz" 2>/dev/null; then
        say "none published for it, so building from source instead"
        rm -rf "$dir"
        return 1
    fi
    if ! tar -xzf "$dir/tiny.tar.gz" -C "$dir" tiny 2>/dev/null; then
        say "could not unpack it, so building instead"
        rm -rf "$dir"
        return 1
    fi
    if ! "$dir/tiny" --version >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        say "it does not run on this system, so building from source instead"
        rm -rf "$dir"
        return 1
    fi
    if ! put_in_place "$dir/tiny"; then
        rm -rf "$dir"
        die "could not put tiny in $PREFIX"
    fi
    rm -rf "$dir"
    say "done"
}

# Running from inside a checkout means "build this", so a checkout never
# downloads.
if ! { [ -f "./Cargo.toml" ] && grep -q 'name = "tiny"' ./Cargo.toml 2>/dev/null; } \
    && prebuilt; then
    finish
    exit 0
fi

# --- a compiler -------------------------------------------------------------
#
# Rust compiles tiny, but it links with the system's C toolchain, which on a
# Mac is Apple's command line tools. macOS answers to `cc` either way: without
# the tools it is a stub, and the build fails at the very end, after every
# crate has compiled, with "invalid active developer path". So ask before
# building, and install them the way macOS itself offers to.
if [ "$(uname -s)" = Darwin ] \
    && ! { dev=$(xcode-select -p 2>/dev/null) && [ -d "$dev" ]; }; then
    say "Building tiny needs Apple's command line tools: the compiler and linker"
    say "macOS installs on request. They are a free download from Apple and"
    say "install in a window of their own. Install them now?"
    ask || die "the command line tools are needed to build: xcode-select --install"
    xcode-select --install >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
    die "finish installing the command line tools in the window that opened, then run this again"
fi

# Linux links with its C compiler too, and tiny compiles a little C of its
# own — the map's parsers, and Lua for plugins. A minimal system often has
# none, and the build would fail at the first crate that needs it.
if [ "$(uname -s)" != Darwin ] && ! { have cc || have gcc || have clang; }; then
    say "Building tiny needs a C compiler, and this system has none."
    pm=$(package_manager)
    [ -n "$pm" ] || die "install gcc (or clang) with your package manager, then run this again"
    say "Install one with $pm now?"
    ask || die "a C compiler is needed to build tiny: install gcc, then run this again"
    install_packages "$pm" cc || die "could not install a C compiler"
fi

# --- rust -------------------------------------------------------------------

if ! have cargo; then
    if [ -x "$HOME/.cargo/bin/cargo" ]; then
        PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH"
    else
        say "tiny is written in Rust, and cargo is not installed."
        say "Install the Rust toolchain now? It goes in ~/.rustup and ~/.cargo,"
        # Single quotes inside: backquotes in a double-quoted string are a
        # command substitution, so this line used to *run* the uninstaller.
        say "and 'rustup self uninstall' removes it again."
        ask || die "cargo is required — see https://rustup.rs"
        have curl || die "curl is required to fetch rustup"
        curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs \
            | sh -s -- -y --profile minimal --default-toolchain stable
        PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH"
    fi
fi
have cargo || die "cargo still not on PATH"

# --- source -----------------------------------------------------------------

if [ -f "./Cargo.toml" ] && grep -q 'name = "tiny"' ./Cargo.toml 2>/dev/null; then
    SRC="$(pwd)"
    say "building from $SRC"
else
    have git || die "git is required to fetch the source"
    SRC="$(temp_dir)" || die "could not make a temporary directory"
    SRC_IS_TEMP=1
    printf 'fetching %s (%s) ... ' "$REPO" "$REF"
    git clone --depth 1 --branch "$REF" "$REPO" "$SRC" >/dev/null 2>&1 \
        || { printf '\n'; die "could not clone $REPO"; }
    say "done"
fi

# --- build ------------------------------------------------------------------

mkdir -p "$PREFIX"

# Turn cargo's running commentary into one line that moves.
#
# The bar is drawn with `\r` and no newline, so the whole build occupies a
# single line however many crates go past. The field holding the crate name is
# padded, because a shorter name has to wipe the longer one it replaced and no
# clear-to-end-of-line escape is worth assuming.
#
# With no total — an old cargo, or a `cargo tree` that failed — it counts
# instead of filling. A bar that cannot say how far along it is should say so
# rather than invent a denominator.
#
# This was an awk script, and the bar arrived in one burst at the end of the
# build. The output was already flushed every frame, so it was not awk's
# writing that was buffered — it was awk's *reading*. mawk, which is `awk` on
# Debian and Ubuntu, fills a several-kilobyte input buffer before it runs a
# single rule, so nothing reached the screen until cargo had printed enough to
# fill it, which for a build is somewhere near the end. A `while read` loop has
# no such buffer: the shell takes one line at a time, which is what a progress
# bar needs and is cheap at the couple of hundred lines cargo prints.
BAR_FULL='############################'
BAR_EMPTY='............................'
BAR_WIDTH=28

# A one-off message in the same place the bar lives. Silent when there is
# nothing to draw on, so the log-file case stays readable.
draw() { if tty_out; then printf '\r  %-52.52s' "$1"; fi; }

# `$1` crates done of `$TOTAL`, and what is happening right now.
bar() {
    if [ "$TOTAL" -le 0 ]; then
        if [ "$1" -eq 1 ]; then
            printf '\r  %d crate   %-30.30s' "$1" "$2"
        else
            printf '\r  %d crates  %-30.30s' "$1" "$2"
        fi
        return 0
    fi
    p=$(( $1 * 100 / TOTAL ))
    if [ "$p" -gt 100 ]; then p=100; fi
    f=$(( p * BAR_WIDTH / 100 ))
    printf '\r  [%.*s%.*s] %3d%%  %-30.30s' \
        "$f" "$BAR_FULL" "$(( BAR_WIDTH - f ))" "$BAR_EMPTY" "$p" "$2"
}

watch_build() {
    if tty_out; then
        n=0
        d=0
        # `|| [ -n "$line" ]` catches a last line with no newline on the end,
        # which `read` reports as failure even though it read something.
        while IFS= read -r line || [ -n "$line" ]; do
            # Cargo indents its verbs by a variable amount to line them up.
            rest=${line#"${line%%[! ]*}"}
            case "$rest" in
                # The sentinel is bookkeeping, not something to show anyone.
                tiny-install-failed*) ;;
                Updating\ *) draw "updating the crate index" ;;
                Downloaded\ *)
                    d=$(( d + 1 ))
                    if [ "$d" -eq 1 ]; then
                        draw "fetched 1 crate"
                    else
                        draw "fetched $d crates"
                    fi
                    ;;
                Compiling\ *)
                    n=$(( n + 1 ))
                    name=${rest#Compiling }
                    name=${name%% *}
                    # tiny is always the last crate: everything it depends on
                    # has to exist before it can be built. So its arrival means
                    # the only work left is the link, however few `Compiling`
                    # lines came before it — which is the ordinary case when
                    # the build directory is warm and the dependencies are all
                    # still there from last time.
                    if [ "$name" = tiny ] && [ "$TOTAL" -gt 0 ]; then
                        bar "$(( TOTAL - 1 ))" "linking tiny"
                    else
                        bar "$n" "compiling $name"
                    fi
                    ;;
                # The end of the build, and the only honest marker of it.
                # `cargo install` prints `Installing tiny v0.3.1` when it
                # *starts* as well as `Installing <path>` when it finishes, so
                # matching on that drew a full bar before the first crate had
                # compiled.
                Finished\ *)
                    # A full bar when there is a total to fill; with no total
                    # the line is a count, and the count is what it is.
                    if [ "$TOTAL" -gt 0 ]; then
                        bar "$TOTAL" "installing"
                    else
                        bar "$n" "installing"
                    fi
                    ;;
            esac
            line=''
        done
        if [ "$n" -gt 0 ] || [ "$d" -gt 0 ]; then printf '\n'; fi
    else
        # Not a terminal: a bar redrawn with carriage returns into a log file
        # is one unreadable line thousands of characters long. Drain it and
        # let the log speak.
        cat >/dev/null
    fi
    # The log is what actually says whether it worked — the loop's exit status
    # is its own, and the shell has no way to reach back for cargo's through a
    # pipe.
    ! grep -q 'tiny-install-failed' "$LOG"
}

# How many crates the bar is counting against.
#
# `cargo tree` lists the packages actually reachable at build time — normal and
# build dependencies, no dev-dependencies — and cargo prints one `Compiling`
# line for each. Asking cargo rather than writing a number down means the bar
# stays right when the dependency list changes, and an old cargo that does not
# know the command just leaves this empty, which turns the bar into a count.
say "building — this takes a minute the first time"
draw "reading the dependency list"
TOTAL=$(cargo tree --manifest-path "$SRC/Cargo.toml" \
            -e normal,build --prefix none --no-dedupe 2>/dev/null \
        | awk 'NF' | sort -u | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
case "$TOTAL" in ''|*[!0-9]*|0) TOTAL=0 ;; esac

LOG="$(temp_file)" || die "could not make a temporary file"

# Cargo says what it is doing on stderr, a line per crate. Reading those is
# what turns "wait for a minute with nothing on screen" into something you can
# watch, and the log keeps the whole of it for the failure case, where what
# went wrong matters more than how far it got.
#
# The sentinel is how a POSIX shell gets the exit status of the first command
# in a pipeline: `$?` is the last one's, and there is no `PIPESTATUS` here.
#
# Cargo installs into `<root>/bin` and keeps its own records in `<root>`, so it
# is given a root of its own, thrown away afterwards, and the binary is moved to
# where it was asked for. Handing it the prefix's parent instead only put the
# binary in the prefix when the prefix happened to be called `bin`.
build() {
    { cargo install --path "$SRC" --bin tiny --root "$ROOT" 2>&1 \
        || echo "tiny-install-failed"; } | tee "$LOG" | watch_build
}

ROOT="$(temp_dir)" || die "could not make a temporary directory"
if ! build; then
    # The sentinel is ours; showing it to someone whose build just failed would
    # only be one more confusing line among the ones that matter.
    say ""
    grep -v 'tiny-install-failed' "$LOG" | tail -n 30 >&2
    die "build failed — the output above says why"
fi

[ -x "$ROOT/bin/tiny" ] || die "the build finished without leaving a binary"
put_in_place "$ROOT/bin/tiny" || die "could not put tiny in $PREFIX"
finish
